notes.meaning: Luke uses the word "we" to show that he sailed along with Paul on this journey. The Roman governor had decided to send Paul to Rome after Paul asked to be tried by the emperor, yet God was guiding the whole event. Paul and several other prisoners were placed under the guard of an officer named Julius, who belonged to an elite unit of Roman soldiers.

The group boarded a ship from the port of Adramyttium that was heading to harbors along the coast of Asia Minor. Aristarchus, a faithful Christian friend from Thessalonica, chose to travel with Paul to support him during his trials. Leaving port, the ship began its voyage north along the coast.

The ship made its first stop at Sidon, about seventy miles north of where they started. Julius showed great kindness to Paul, trusting him enough to let him go ashore to visit fellow believers and receive their help and supplies. Paul kept his word and returned to custody rather than trying to run away.

Strong headwinds from the west made it impossible to sail straight across the open sea toward Italy. To protect the ship from the rough wind, the crew steered along the sheltered side of the large island of Cyprus. This path kept the island between the ship and the strong gusts.

The ship sailed across the open waters off the coasts of Cilicia and Pamphylia, where coastal currents helped them make progress. They eventually reached the port of Myra in the region of Lycia. Myra was an important coastal stop where larger ships could often be found.

At Myra, the centurion found a large cargo ship from Alexandria in Egypt that was carrying grain directly to Italy. Julius transferred Paul, the other prisoners, and the soldiers onto this new vessel to continue the journey to Rome.

The heavy grain ship made slow and difficult progress for many days because of stubborn opposing winds. When they could not get into the harbor at Cnidus, the wind forced them south toward the island of Crete, where they rounded Cape Salmone to find shelter on the island's southern side.

The crew struggled along the coast of Crete with great effort until they reached a bay called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea. While this bay gave temporary relief from the wind, it was not a safe harbor for a ship to remain in all winter.

The crew had lost a great deal of time fighting contrary winds, and open-sea sailing had become very risky. "The Fast" refers to the Jewish Day of Atonement in early autumn, a yearly day of fasting (going without food to pray and seek God's mercy), after which severe winter storms regularly began. Realizing the danger, Paul urged the leaders to stop the voyage.

Paul told the men plainly that continuing the voyage would bring disaster, wrecking the vessel and ruining the cargo. He also warned them that their very lives would be placed in terrible danger if they pushed ahead.

The centurion had the final say, but he chose to trust the professional pilot and the ship's owner instead of listening to Paul. The ship's leaders thought experienced sailors knew better than a prisoner, choosing worldly judgment over the warning God had prompted Paul to give.

Fair Havens was exposed to harsh winter winds, making it an unpleasant and risky place to remain for months. The majority of the crew voted to put out to sea again, hoping they could reach Phoenix, a nearby Cretan harbor that faced away from the worst storm winds.

A gentle breeze began to blow from the south, leading the crew to think their plan had succeeded. They pulled up the anchor and sailed close along the shoreline of Crete, expecting an easy trip to Phoenix.

The calm weather did not last long before a violent, whirling wind called the Northeaster suddenly swept down from the mountains of Crete. This fierce gale rushed out over the water and struck the ship with hurricane force.

The tempest was so fierce that the vessel could not turn into the wind or hold its course. Realizing they could not fight the storm, the sailors stopped trying to steer and let the ship be driven along by the waves.

The ship drifted past the sheltered side of a tiny island named Cauda, where the water was slightly calmer. In those few moments of protection, the men worked with great difficulty to haul aboard the trailing lifeboat before it could be smashed or sunk.

Once the lifeboat was secured, the crew wrapped heavy ropes around the hull of the ship to keep its planks from bursting apart under the pounding of the sea. Terrified that the wind would push them onto the treacherous sandbars of Syrtis near Africa, they lowered the sails and gear, allowing the vessel to drift.

The storm battered the ship so violently that it began to take on water and threatened to sink. The next day, the crew began throwing commercial freight overboard to lighten the ship and keep it afloat.

By the third day, the crisis was so desperate that ordinary passengers had to join the crew in hard labor. With their own hands, they cast the ship's spare tackle, ropes, and heavy equipment into the raging sea.

Thick storm clouds completely hid the sun by day and the stars by night for a long time. Because ancient sailors relied on the sun and stars to navigate, the crew was totally lost in the dark, and all hope of surviving was finally abandoned.

The people on board had gone without food for many days because of sickness, terror, and the impossibility of cooking during the violent storm. Paul stepped forward and reminded them that they should have listened to his warning in Crete, pointing to their present losses not to gloat, but to urge them to trust what he would say next.
Paul told the despairing travelers to cheer up and take courage. Even though the ship would be broken to pieces, he gave them the remarkable assurance that not a single human life would be lost.
